actions.name: Review vital signs flowsheet
actions.result: BP 128/82 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, Temp 98.6°F, RR 16/min, measured at last clinic visit (home cuff not used today).

actions.name: Review anthropometric data
actions.result: Height 5'9" (175 cm), Weight 178 lbs (80.7 kg), BMI 27.8 kg/m² (overweight), weight up 5 lbs over past 3 months.

actions.name: Review HbA1c
actions.result: HbA1c 9.8% (goal <7.0%) — poorly controlled, drawn 1 week ago.

actions.name: Review lipid panel
actions.result: Total cholesterol 220 mg/dL (ref <200 mg/dL) — mildly elevated; LDL and triglycerides also flagged high on report.

actions.name: Review medication list
actions.result: Metformin 500mg once daily (poor adherence, intermittent), Lisinopril 10mg once daily (fair adherence); OTC vitamin C occasional; mother-recommended 'cojiro root' tea.

actions.name: Review problem list / recent history
actions.result: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (poorly controlled), history of prediabetes x2 years, s/p gunshot wound with emergency surgery 2 months ago (recovering), hypertension.

actions.name: Take 24-hour dietary recall
actions.result: Patient reports: often skips breakfast; lunch is rice, beans, sometimes pork or pre-made food from a nearby stand; dinner with family includes rice, beans, plantains, occasional pork, coconut milk dishes; drinks pineapple juice ('jus de piña') and soda through the day, minimal plain water; snacks on sweet treats like quesillos in the evening, especially when stressed or can't sleep.

actions.name: Assess meal pattern and timing
actions.result: Irregular meal timing tied to work schedule; breakfast frequently skipped; lunch and dinner timing variable; no planned snacks around medication dosing.

actions.name: Assess hydration habits
actions.result: High intake of sugar-sweetened beverages (juice, soda); reports drinking very little plain water most days.

actions.name: Assess physical activity level
actions.result: Low-to-moderate activity; walks for community volunteer work; no structured exercise program; reports feeling fatigued and some residual weakness from surgery recovery.

actions.name: Assess food access and affordability
actions.result: Reports inconsistent work hours affect food budget and meal planning; relies on pre-made/convenience foods at times; neighborhood has limited fresh produce access (food desert characteristics).

actions.name: Assess medication-food interaction and side effects
actions.result: Patient reports mild GI upset (nausea/loose stools) with metformin, inconsistent timing with meals, which contributes to skipping doses.

actions.name: Assess readiness to change / stage of change
actions.result: Patient expresses ambivalence; open to small, practical changes if he perceives quick, tangible benefit; skeptical of generic medical advice.

actions.name: Screen for disordered eating patterns
actions.result: On further gentle questioning patient discloses a past period of restrictive eating tied to body image and family stress; currently not actively restricting but history noted for care team awareness.

actions.name: Screen for sleep and stress impact on eating
actions.result: Patient reports poor sleep quality, trauma-related stress (nightmares, hypervigilance) since the shooting, and that late-night eating/snacking is tied to difficulty sleeping and stress.

actions.name: Review family/social history
actions.result: Mother has type 2 diabetes; patient lives with parents and younger siblings; strong family and community ties; identifies as primary motivator to protect/provide for siblings.

actions.name: Explore cultural food beliefs and trust in care team
actions.result: Patient states he trusts his mother's home remedies more than doctors, feels prior hospital experience was dismissive of his culture, and believes diet alone (not meds) should control his sugar.

cells: Lower blood glucose, improve insulin sensitivity
Poor - intermittent, often forgotten/skipped due to GI upset
Believed by family to help lower sugar

artifacts.title: Discharge Summary - Trauma Surgery (2 months ago)
artifacts.author: Trauma Surgery Service
artifacts.body: 22-year-old male s/p gunshot wound to the left lower abdomen, underwent emergency exploratory laparotomy with repair of small bowel injury. Post-operative course uncomplicated. Discharged on post-op day 6 with home health follow-up. Advised gradual return to activity. Pre-existing history of prediabetes noted; patient counseled at discharge to follow up with primary care for diabetes monitoring given stress-related hyperglycemia risk during recovery. Patient reported understanding but appeared distracted and eager to leave; limited engagement with discharge teaching noted by nursing staff.

objectives.text: Apply the Nutrition Care Process by conducting a comprehensive assessment including diet history, anthropometrics, labs, lifestyle, and social/financial barriers.
Formulate an accurate, patient-specific PES statement linking the nutrition diagnosis to etiology (barriers/beliefs) and signs/symptoms (labs, intake pattern).

Design culturally relevant, practical nutrition interventions (e.g., modified Puerto Rican meal pattern, hydration swaps, carbohydrate consistency) that respect food preferences and financial constraints.
Integrate medication adherence and side-effect management into nutrition counseling, addressing metformin timing with meals.
Use motivational interviewing techniques (open-ended questions, reflective listening, affirmations) to explore ambivalence, build trust, and elicit the patient's own motivators for change.

Identify lifestyle, psychosocial, and trauma-related barriers (stress, sleep, mistrust, financial strain) that affect eating behavior and glycemic control, and consider interprofessional/community referrals.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Altered nutrition-related laboratory values (hyperglycemia) related to poorly controlled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
differential: Excessive carbohydrate/sugar-sweetened beverage intake related to limited access to affordable healthy foods and irregular work schedule, as evidenced by elevated HbA1c (9.8%) and fasting glucose (180 mg/dL)
Inconsistent medication-nutrition therapy related to GI side effects of metformin and distrust of pharmacologic treatment, as evidenced by self-reported intermittent dosing

Undesirable food choices related to food and nutrition-related knowledge deficit concerning carbohydrate quality and portion, as evidenced by frequent intake of sugary beverages and refined-carbohydrate convenience foods
Disordered eating pattern (resolved/at risk) related to trauma history and body image concerns, as evidenced by self-reported past restrictive eating episode
keyFindings: HbA1c 9.8% (goal <7%), rising sharply over past 6 months from 6.8% a year ago
BMI 27.8 (overweight), 5 lb weight gain over 3 months after post-surgical weight loss
Elevated total cholesterol 220 mg/dL, LDL 142, low HDL 38, triglycerides 195
High intake of sugar-sweetened beverages (juice, soda), low water intake
Skips breakfast frequently due to cost; irregular meal timing tied to inconsistent work hours
Poor metformin adherence due to GI side effects and belief diet alone will fix his sugar
Food access barriers consistent with living in a food desert; financial strain limits fresh produce purchases
Trauma-related stress and poor sleep contributing to late-night/stress eating
History of disordered eating related to body image, currently not active but relevant to monitor
Strong mistrust of healthcare system; trusts mother's home remedies over medical advice
Protective motivation toward younger siblings identified as potential lever for behavior change
plan: Negotiate one or two small, achievable first changes (e.g., swap one sugary drink/day for water or unsweetened agua fresca) rather than a full diet overhaul
Provide carbohydrate-consistency education using familiar Puerto Rican foods (rice, beans, plantains) with portion guidance rather than elimination
Discuss timing metformin with a meal to reduce GI upset and improve adherence; coordinate with prescriber if side effects persist
Address hydration: reduce sugar-sweetened beverages, increase plain water, suggest infused water as a culturally acceptable alternative
Explore affordable protein/fiber sources and low-cost strategies for breakfast given financial constraints and food desert context
Validate and leverage his motivation to protect/care for siblings and resume community volunteer work as change drivers

Screen further for PTSD-related sleep disruption and refer to behavioral health/trauma-informed counseling as appropriate; consider referral to social work for food assistance programs (SNAP equivalent, community food bank)
Build trust using motivational interviewing: open-ended questions, reflective listening, avoid directive/judgmental language about non-adherence
Schedule close follow-up (2-4 weeks) to reassess glucose logs, reinforce small wins, and adjust plan collaboratively
Involve family (mother) respectfully in education given her influence, offering to discuss culturally-relevant remedies without dismissing them outright
redFlags: HbA1c rapidly worsening (6.8% to 9.8% in 6 months) suggesting urgent need for intensified glycemic management
Symptoms of hyperglycemia present (polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue, blurred vision) warranting prompt communication with prescriber about possible medication adjustment
History of disordered eating requires sensitive monitoring to avoid triggering restrictive patterns with diabetes diet teaching
Trauma-related stress/possible PTSD symptoms affecting sleep and eating - mental health referral indicated
Financial/food insecurity may undermine any nutrition intervention if not addressed concurrently
educationPoints: Explain HbA1c and fasting glucose in plain language and what the numbers mean for his goals (playing with siblings, returning to work)
Teach carbohydrate consistency and glycemic impact of sugar-sweetened beverages using his own foods as examples, not foreign substitutions
Clarify that diet and medication work together, not diet 'versus' medication, respecting his belief while gently correcting misinformation
Discuss metformin-food timing to reduce GI side effects and improve adherence without shaming him for missed doses
Provide practical, low-literacy, visual tools (plate method using rice/beans/plantain proportions) rather than complex carb-counting
Acknowledge and respect his mother's home remedies while discussing what is known/unknown about their effect on blood sugar
Normalize that trauma recovery affects appetite, sleep, and stress eating, and that support is available without judgment

profile.title: Poorly Controlled Type 2 Diabetes in a 22-Year-Old Trauma Survivor with Healthcare Mistrust
profile.summary: A 22-year-old Puerto Rican man with a 2-year history of prediabetes, now poorly controlled Type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9.8%), presents for a telehealth nutrition visit 2 months after emergency surgery for a gunshot wound. The case challenges learners to perform a culturally sensitive nutrition assessment, uncover financial and trauma-related barriers to self-care, and use motivational interviewing to engage a skeptical, low-adherence patient in realistic, culturally congruent dietary change.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in an urban Latino neighborhood in Puerto Rico, using a smartphone propped on a kitchen table

patient.name: Dominic Rivera
patient.occupation: Part-time community volunteer and college student (associate degree seeking)
patient.appearance: Sitting at a kitchen table in a small apartment, wearing a community-volunteer T-shirt, looks tired with mild under-eye circles, arms crossed at first, phone propped against a stack of books; occasionally glances off-screen when a younger sibling's voice is heard in the background

persona.personality: Resilient, pragmatic, protective of family, skeptical of authority, masks vulnerability with bluntness
persona.communicationStyle: Direct and occasionally blunt, uses slang, may interrupt if feeling unheard, switches to English for clinical topics but prefers Spanish, opens up when respected
persona.emotionalState: Guarded and slightly defensive at first, with underlying fatigue and stress; softens when discussion turns to his siblings or community work
persona.background: Grew up in an urban Latino neighborhood in Puerto Rico, lives with his parents and younger siblings, volunteers in his community helping neighbors, is working toward an associate degree part-time, recently survived a shooting and underwent emergency abdominal surgery two months ago, has a pet dog he walks daily, attends a weekly community meeting about local issues
speechExamples: Look, I take the metformin when I remember, okay? It's not like it's magic.
My mom's tea has worked for people in my family for years, so don't tell me it's nothing.
I just want to be able to play with my little brother and sister without getting dizzy.
You guys always say 'eat better' like it's that easy when I'm working whenever they call me in.
I'm not trying to end up back in that hospital, trust me.
concerns: Fear of losing his volunteer position if his health doesn't improve
Fear of becoming a burden on his family
Wanting quick, visible results from any changes he makes

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition follow-up visit with Dominic Rivera, a 22-year-old man with poorly controlled Type 2 diabetes (recent HbA1c 9.8%), recovering from a gunshot wound 2 months ago. He was referred for nutrition counseling due to worsening glycemic control. Review his chart before the call. Your goals are to complete a nutrition assessment, identify barriers to self-management, and begin culturally sensitive, patient-centered counseling.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referred for nutrition counseling due to poorly controlled Type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9.8%) and recent weight gain
scenario.openingLine: Yeah, hi... they said I had to do this nutrition call because my sugar's high again. I don't got a lot of time though, I gotta pick up my sister soon.
tasks: Conduct a thorough diet history and 24-hour recall, including beverages, snacking, and meal timing
Identify social, financial, and cultural barriers affecting his nutrition and diabetes self-management
Explore medication adherence issues and their relationship to diet/side effects using a non-judgmental approach
Apply motivational interviewing techniques to assess readiness to change and elicit his personal motivators
Formulate a PES statement and propose at least one culturally appropriate, practical nutrition intervention

facts.chart: Patient aware he was referred for nutrition counseling due to high blood sugar
facts.says: Yeah, hi... they said I had to do this nutrition call because my sugar's high again.

facts.chart: Reports frequent thirst, urination, fatigue, occasional sweet cravings, occasional mild headache and blurred vision
facts.says: I'm thirsty all the time lately, and tired, like really tired. Sometimes my head hurts a little and things get blurry for a sec.

facts.chart: Reports skipping metformin doses frequently, takes it inconsistently
facts.says: Look, I take the metformin when I remember, okay? It's not like it's magic.

facts.chart: Reports usual intake of rice and beans most days
facts.says: Mostly I eat rice and beans, that's just how we eat here.

facts.chart: Reports recent gunshot wound and surgery 2 months ago, recovering
facts.says: I got shot a couple months back, had surgery and everything. Still recovering.

facts.chart: Mentions a sibling is currently ill
facts.says: My little sister's been sick lately too, it's a lot going on at home.

facts.chart: States preference for juice over water
facts.says: Honestly I like juice way more than water. The piña juice especially.

facts.chart: Reports irregular work/volunteer hours affecting routine
facts.says: My hours are all over the place, they call me whenever they need me for the community stuff.

facts.chart: States he trusts his mother's advice more than doctors
facts.says: I trust my mom more than I trust you guys, no offense. Her advice has worked before.

facts.chart: Reports skipping breakfast regularly
facts.says: I usually don't eat breakfast, I just grab something small or nothing at all.

facts.chart: Adherence tied to how he's feeling that day; takes metformin only on 'good days'
facts.says: If I'm feeling okay that day, I'll take it. If not, I just forget or don't bother.

facts.chart: Reports late-night snacking on sweets like quesillos
facts.says: Yeah, sometimes at night I'll have a quesillo or something sweet, especially if I can't sleep.

facts.chart: States goal of lowering blood sugar to be active with younger siblings
facts.says: I just want to be able to play with my little brother and sister without getting dizzy.

facts.chart: Reveals skips breakfast partly to save money for lunch
facts.says: ...honestly, sometimes I skip breakfast so I have enough for lunch, money's tight.

facts.chart: Acknowledges trauma-related stress affects his eating habits, especially at night
facts.says: Since... everything happened, I don't sleep right, and that's when I end up eating stuff I shouldn't.

facts.chart: Admits he wants to be more active but feels too weak/fatigued from recovery
facts.says: I want to move more, walk more, but I get tired fast still, since the surgery.

facts.chart: Downplays but eventually admits fear of being a burden to his family
facts.says: I don't want to be... like, a problem for my family, you know? I'm supposed to help them, not the other way around.

facts.chart: Reports mild GI upset with metformin contributing to non-adherence
facts.says: That metformin messes with my stomach sometimes, so I just skip it those days.

facts.chart: Believes sugar is not the only cause of his diabetes, skeptical of standard advice
facts.says: Sugar's not the only thing that causes this, my mom didn't eat sweets and she got it too.

facts.chart: Relies on pre-made or convenience foods often since recovering from surgery
facts.says: I don't cook much right now, still healing, so I grab stuff that's already made a lot of the time.

facts.chart: States goal to return to volunteer work and regain independence
facts.says: I just want to get back to my volunteer stuff and not depend on everybody for everything.

facts.chart: Reports poor sleep quality related to stress/trauma symptoms
facts.says: I don't really sleep good anymore, lots on my mind since the... incident.

facts.chart: Reveals trauma-related stress symptoms (hypervigilance, nightmares) affecting daily function including eating
facts.says: I get these nightmares sometimes, and I'm just... on edge a lot. Makes it hard to eat regular, honestly.

facts.chart: Reports limited access to fresh produce in his neighborhood
facts.says: There's not really a good grocery store close by, mostly little shops with chips and stuff.

facts.chart: States fear of returning to hospital
facts.says: I'm not trying to end up back in that hospital, trust me.

facts.chart: Mother has type 2 diabetes
facts.says: My mom's got the sugar too, has for years.

facts.chart: Identifies strongly with his role as community volunteer and protector of siblings
facts.says: People in the neighborhood count on me, and so do my little siblings. That's just who I am.

facts.chart: History of a period of restrictive eating related to body image and family stress, not currently active
facts.says: ...there was a time, a while back, I barely ate anything, was going through some stuff with how I looked and family drama. I don't really talk about that.

facts.chart: Admits to using an herbal supplement (mother's recommended root tea) believing it may lower blood sugar, aware it's not proven
facts.says: I drink this root tea my mom makes, she swears it helps the sugar. I know it's probably not 'real medicine' but I still drink it.

facts.chart: Holds strong cultural belief that he should be the provider for his family, not a dependent
facts.says: In my family, the men are supposed to take care of everyone else. I'm not supposed to be the one needing help.

facts.chart: Discloses significant financial strain limiting consistent access to healthy food
facts.says: Money's really tight right now, I'm not always able to buy the stuff that's actually good for me.

facts.chart: Denies tobacco or alcohol use
facts.says: No, I don't smoke or drink, never really got into that.

facts.chart: Has a pet dog he walks daily; distractor, not clinically relevant to diabetes management beyond mild activity
facts.says: I got a dog, I walk him most days, he keeps me company.

facts.chart: Attends a weekly community meeting about local issues; distractor detail about his routine
facts.says: I go to this community meeting every week, we talk about stuff happening in the neighborhood.

facts.chart: Takes vitamin C supplement occasionally; distractor, not significantly relevant to glycemic control
facts.says: I take vitamin C sometimes too, just figured it couldn't hurt.
